extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students studying probability and Markov chains (readers of a graduate-level stochastic processes/Markov chains textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, theorems, and definitions for determining recurrence/transience of random walks and for existence, construction, and uniqueness of stationary and reversible measures for Markov chains, together with asymptotic convergence results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence from Gaussian scaling limit (Theorem 5.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S_n is a random walk in R^2 and S_n / n^{1/2} ⇒ a non-degenerate normal distribution then S_n is recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: the conclusion also holds if the limit is degenerate (in that case the walk is essentially lower-dimensional and Chung–Fuchs applies). Proof sketch: use local limit behavior (densities of limit law), Fatou's lemma, and divergence of an integral derived from the normal density near 0 to deduce infinite expected returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier integral recurrence criterion (Theorem 5.4.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let δ > 0. S_n is recurrent if and only if ∫_{(-δ,δ)^d} Re(1 / (1 − φ(y))) dy = ∞, where φ = E e^{i t·X_1} is the characteristic function of one step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a necessary and sufficient analytic criterion based on the behaviour of the characteristic function near 0. (The text proves a slightly weaker but useful variant next.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremum (weaker) Fourier recurrence criterion (Theorem 5.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let δ > 0. S_n is recurrent iff ∫_{(-δ,δ)^d} sup_{r<1} Re(1 / (1 − r φ(y))) dy = ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This weaker form is easier to prove. Note: if the integral in Theorem 5.4.10 is infinite then Fatou's lemma applied to the sup_{r<1} version yields recurrence. The converse (stronger result) requires more advanced arguments (Ornstein 1969, Stone 1969) using reductions to densities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parseval relation for characteristic functions (Lemma 5.4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ and ν are probability measures on R^d with characteristic functions ϕ and ψ, then ∫ ψ(t) µ(dt) = ∫ ϕ(x) ν(dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Fubini's theorem using boundedness of e^{i t·x}. Used to relate probabilities (via convolutions/integrals) to characteristic functions in estimates for recurrence/transience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosine lower bound (Lemma 5.4.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |x| ≤ π/3 then 1 − cos x ≥ x^2 / 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple calculus inequality used to lower bound expressions of the form 1 − cos(·) by quadratic terms; useful when converting characteristic-function expressions to polynomial-like behaviour near 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of test densities to bound local probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounds of the form P(‖S_n‖ < 1/δ) ≤ constant × ∫_{(-δ,δ)^d} product_{i=1}^d (1 − |x_i|/δ)/δ^2 × ϕ_n(x) dx and corresponding lower bounds using other test densities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: choose auxiliary densities with known characteristic functions, apply Lemmas 5.4.12 and 5.4.13, then sum in n (sometimes after multiplying by r^n, r<1) and let r→1. This connects local probabilities to the integrals appearing in the Fourier recurrence criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable-law parameter criterion in d=1 (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For symmetric stable laws with characteristic function ϕ(t) = exp(−|t|^α): the associated random walk is transient for α < 1 and recurrent for α ≥ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: 1 − exp(−|t|^α) ∼ |t|^α as t→0, so apply Theorem 5.4.11. For α > 1 mean 0 gives recurrence via other theorems; α = 1 (Cauchy) is handled directly by the Fourier criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable-law parameter criterion in d=2 (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For planar symmetric stable laws ϕ(t) = exp(−|t|^α) with α < 2, the corresponding random walks are transient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change to polar coordinates and check integrability: ∫_0^δ ρ^{1−α} dρ < ∞ when 1 − α > −1 (i.e., α < 2), giving transience by Theorem 5.4.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: No recurrence in truly three-dimensional walks (Theorem 5.4.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: A random walk in R^3 that is 'truly three-dimensional' (i.e., the distribution of X_1 satisfies P(X_1·θ ≠ 0) > 0 for all θ ≠ 0) is not recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to showing Re(1 − φ(ρ θ)) ≥ C ρ^2 for small ρ uniformly in θ, so the integral in the Fourier recurrence criterion converges for d > 2. Uses Lemma 5.4.13 and Fatou's lemma plus compactness arguments over the sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion formula for lattice walks (Zd)
rubrics_metrics.description: For random walk on Z^d, P(S_n = 0) = (2π)^{-d} ∫_{(-π,π)^d} φ(t)^n dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula allows exact (or table/elliptic-integral) evaluation of sums ∑_n P(S_n=0) via integrals of 1/(1 − r φ(t)) and is used to compute return probabilities for simple random walks on lattices (e.g., Watson's integral evaluation for d=3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of stationary measure / stationary distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure µ is stationary if ∑_x µ(x) p(x,y) = µ(y) (equivalently µ p = µ). If µ is a probability measure it is a stationary distribution: starting X_0 ∼ µ implies X_n ∼ µ for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: µ describes an equilibrium distribution (finite or infinite mass allowed); many results (construction, uniqueness up to constant, relations with recurrence) follow from this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubly-stochastic transitions ⇒ uniform stationary measure
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑_x p(x,y) = 1 for all y (transition matrix is doubly stochastic), then µ(x) ≡ 1 is a stationary measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both necessary and sufficient for µ ≡ 1 to be stationary. Useful quick check in examples like symmetric random walk on Z^d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed balance / reversibility condition
rubrics_metrics.description: µ satisfies detailed balance (is reversible) if µ(x) p(x,y) = µ(y) p(y,x) for all x,y. A reversible measure is stationary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical interpretation: mass transported x→y equals mass transported y→x. If µ is reversible then the time-reversed chain has the same transition probabilities. Useful for constructing stationary measures and exploiting symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual (time-reversed) transition probabilities (Theorem 5.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ is stationary and X_0 ∼ µ, then the time-reversed chain Y_m = X_{n−m} is Markov with transition q(x,y) = µ(y) p(y,x) / µ(x). If µ is reversible, q = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides explicit formula for the backward chain and explains why (and when) reversibility implies identical forward/backward dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov cycle condition for reversibility (Theorem 5.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For irreducible p, existence of a reversible measure is equivalent to (i) p(x,y) > 0 ⇒ p(y,x) > 0, and (ii) for any loop x_0,x_1,...,x_n=x_0 with ∏_{i=1}^n p(x_i,x_{i−1}) > 0, we have ∏_{i=1}^n [p(x_{i−1},x_i) / p(x_i,x_{i−1})] = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a path-independent ratio definition for µ: pick a base state a with µ(a)=1 and define µ(x) by a product of transition ratio factors along any path; cycle condition ensures independence of path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle trick: construct stationary measure from expected visits (Theorem 5.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is a recurrent state and T = inf{n ≥ 1: X_n = x}, then µ_x(y) = E_x[∑_{n=0}^{T−1} 1_{X_n = y}] = ∑_{n=0}^∞ P_x(X_n = y, T > n) defines a stationary measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: µ_x(y) is expected number of visits to y during one cycle returning to x. Proof uses Fubini and the Markov property; called the 'cycle trick'. Ensures existence of a stationary measure supported on the recurrent class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of stationary measure in irreducible recurrent chains (Theorem 5.5.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible and recurrent (all states recurrent) then the stationary measure is unique up to constant multiples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof compares any stationary measure ν to µ_a constructed by the cycle trick from a fixed a and shows equality up to constant multiple by irreducibility and comparison of expected visit counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary distribution implies recurrence of states with positive mass (Theorem 5.5.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a stationary distribution π and π(y) > 0, then state y is recurrent (ρ_{yy} = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses π p^n = π and summation interchange (Fubini) to show ∑_n p_n(x,y) = ∞ when π(y)>0, hence returns happen infinitely often in expectation and recurrence follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary distribution and mean return times relation (Theorem 5.5.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible and has stationary distribution π then π(x) = 1 / E_x T_x (mean return time to x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses µ_x from cycle trick and uniqueness up to scaling; gives the probabilistic meaning of π in terms of average fraction of time spent at x. Implies positive recurrence ⇔ finite mean return time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of positive recurrence and existence of stationary distribution (Theorem 5.5.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For irreducible p the following are equivalent: (i) some x is positive recurrent (E_x T_x < ∞), (ii) there is a stationary distribution, (iii) all states are positive recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus positive recurrence is a class property; existence of a stationary distribution characterizes positive recurrence in irreducible chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any stationary measure is a scalar multiple of a stationary distribution in irreducible positive-recurrent chains (Theorem 5.5.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible and has a stationary distribution π then any other stationary measure is a multiple of π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses an entropy functional with a concave function and Jensen's inequality to show strict convexity unless the ratio µ/π is constant on communicating states; technical reduction by using aperiodicized powers of p when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of period and aperiodicity (Lemmas 5.6.4–5.6.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For recurrent x define I_x = {n ≥ 1 : p_n(x,x) > 0} and d_x = gcd(I_x) the period. Lemma: period is a class property (if ρ_{xy} > 0 then d_y = d_x). If d_x = 1 (aperiodic) then p_m(x,x) > 0 for all sufficiently large m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aperiodicity (d=1) is important for convergence to equilibrium; easy checks: p(x,x)>0 implies aperiodicity; number-theoretic argument ensures eventual return times fill all large integers once gcd=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence to stationary distribution for irreducible aperiodic chains (Theorem 5.6.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible, aperiodic, and has stationary distribution π, then p_n(x,y) → π(y) as n → ∞ for every x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via coupling: run two independent copies until they meet (or couple) and show total variation distance ≤ 2 P(T > n) → 0. Construction of a product chain on S×S and hitting the diagonal gives the required coupling. For finite-state irreducible aperiodic chains this yields exponential convergence (see exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong law for occupation counts (Theorem 5.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If y is recurrent, then for any x ∈ S, N_n(y)/n → (1 / E_y T_y) 1_{T_y < ∞} almost surely under P_x (with 1/∞ = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: long-run fraction of time spent at y equals reciprocal of mean return time when return times are finite (positive recurrence); used to justify the names positive/null recurrent.
